title: DOJ Takes Paramount’s Side Against States in Fight Over $1.9 Billion Bond
description: The Department of Justice sided with Paramount on Tuesday, arguing that a coalition of 12 states should be forced to post a bond as the price of con
body:
The Department of Justice sided with Paramount on Tuesday, arguing that a coalition of 12 states should be forced to post a bond as the price of continuing to block the Warner Bros. merger.

	Paramount has argued that it stands to lose at least $1.88 billion due to the delay resulting from the states’ antitrust lawsuit. The company has asked Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin to require the states to post a bond in that amount, which would compensate the company in the event that it prevails at trial.
	

	The DOJ is not a party to the state litigation, but filed a “statement of interest” in the case on Tuesday. The document argues that the states must post a “proper bond” because they are acting in the role of “private persons” in enforcing federal antitrust law.


	The DOJ approved the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger in June and issued an unusual and lengthy statement explaining its support for the transaction. The 12-state coalition, led by California, reached the opposite conclusion in July, filing suit to prevent the merger from reducing competition in the theatrical and basic cable markets. A trial is scheduled to begin on March 2.

	Paramount voluntarily agreed not to close the deal until after a trial is held back in July. At the time, Martinez-Olguin had issued a 28-day temporary restraining order, but had not imposed an injunction that would block the deal indefinitely.

	Rather than fight an injunction motion — and potentially be forced to appeal an adverse ruling — Paramount chose instead to concede the issue and concentrate its trial defense. But the company had a change of heart in August, arguing that the states should be forced to post the bond or, in the alternative, allow the merger to proceed.
	

	In opposing Paramount’s request, the states noted that courts routinely waive the bond requirement when states are suing to enforce public interests. Martinez-Olguin waived the requirement to post a bond when she granted the temporary restraining order.

	The states also argued that requiring states to post a bond would gut their enforcement power. They also argued that Paramount had given no reason why the court should rewrite a stipulation that Paramount had voluntarily acceded to less than a month earlier.

	“Permitting Paramount to enter the stipulation and then rewrite it almost immediately would allow it to unfairly renege on its commitments,” the states argued. “Paramount has failed to show any change in circumstances that would justify its attempt now to rewrite the terms of the stipulation it submitted to the Court.”

	A hearing on the bond request is set for Sept. 24.

	Paramount has separately challenged whether the states have authority to enforce federal antitrust law at all. In a filing last week, the company suggested that one of its defenses will be that such authority “is vested in the U.S. Department of Justice.”

schema.headline: DOJ Takes Paramount’s Side Against States in Fight Over $1.9 Billion Bond

title: Taylor Frankie Paul Sets Return to ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Following Chaotic Season 5 and Ongoing Legal Battle
description:
Taylor Frankie Paul is returning to production on “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.”

	Though Hulu declined to comment on Paul’s involvement in Sea
body:
Taylor Frankie Paul is returning to production on “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives.”

	Though Hulu declined to comment on Paul’s involvement in Season 6, Variety confirmed the news with multiple sources after it was implied in social media posts from cast member Mikayla Matthews, who announced she was quitting the show on Sept. 14.

	Outside of her Season 5 confessionals, Paul hasn’t shot new material for the reality show since March, when production was put on pause due to a police investigation into domestic violence allegations she and her ex-boyfriend Dakota Mortensen made against each other. Shortly thereafter, TMZ released video from a separate domestic incident between them, which led ABC to cancel her season of “The Bachelorette.” Paul and Mortensen have made additional allegations against each other in the months since, leading to mutual restraining orders and a battle for custody over their shared son, Ever. (No charges have been filed in the matter.)
	

	Season 6 recently entered production without Paul. But on Monday, Matthews shared in an Instagram post saying that she was leaving the show after receiving news that upset her, which she implied was related to Paul. On Tuesday, she made another post all but confirming that her exit was a moral objection to Paul’s return.

	Though Matthews didn’t mention Paul by name, she wrote, “The ONLY reason I’m leaving the show is because I was told a certain person was coming back. I told them before agreeing to do 6 that I wasn’t going to film if that certain someone came back. Because it’s UNETHICAL and kids are involved. And I’m being put in an unfair position because of the things I’ve seen and heard that I don’t agree with.”
	

	“Mormon Wives” cast members Mayci Neeley and Layla Taylor may be next to jump ship. Both left comments of support on Matthews’ initial post, and told fans their futures with the show were unclear. “I am finishing this current season that we are filming and then not sure for after that,” Neeley wrote in a TikTok comment after being asked about her status. She then posted a video about material that was cut from the recently released Season 5 with a caption that read, “At the end of the day I don’t care about having ‘aura’ I care about providing for my family and being a good wife/ mother. Period. Going into SLOMW my intention has never been the fame, it has always been $$$ to provide for my fam and to positively impact people by sharing my story. So I’ll take the cut and stay happy & healed.” Responding to a similar fan question about Matthews’ exit, Taylor wrote, “I just love her so much. It’s such an impossible situation for everyone involved, but I am finishing season 6 and then tbd.”

schema.headline: Taylor Frankie Paul Sets Return to ‘The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Following Chaotic Season 5 and Ongoing Legal Battle

title: How Competitive ‘Pokémon’ Inspired Author Ava Reid’s New Dystopian YA Series ‘Winterveil’
description: It’s the start of another dark academia season and fantasy author Ava Reid (“A Study in Drowning,” “Innamorata”) is celebrating with the release of
body:
It’s the start of another dark academia season and fantasy author Ava Reid (“A Study in Drowning,” “Innamorata”) is celebrating with the release of her new YA dystopian novel, “Winterveil.”

	The first book in a planned duology, “Winterveil” is set at Valeran Academy, which boasts the brightest – and precociously criminal – students in the nation, who are trained to be elite assets in a Cold War that has dragged on for nearly a century. Amid eerie war simulations, cutthroat competitions and foreboding new technology, four students are drawn together for a mysterious mission.
	

	Without getting into spoilers, we can reveal this political tale has one particular inspiration that might come as a surprise: competitive “Pokémon.”


	“I, like so many of us, grew up playing ‘Pokémon’ as a kid,” Reid tells Variety. “Playing ‘FireRed,’ ‘LeafGreen.’ I have all my Pokemon plushies right behind me on my couch right now. But it was during the pandemic that I think so many of us got very involved in kind of esoteric hobbies, and my hobby that I got really into during COVID was competitive ‘Pokémon,’ specifically.”

	And that’s what it sounds like, according to Reid, “’Pokémon’ where you play against you know other players and you have battles.” “And I’m talking specifically about the official competitive format of Pokemon, the one that’s run by the Pokémon Company itself,” Reid says. “There are different fan formats where you can play online, but the official competitive format is called VGC. So I got very, very into VGC, watching a bunch of kind of VGC content creators, playing on the in-game ladder myself.” 
	

	Reid’s time spent playing some hard core Pokemon inspired aspects of the competitive nature of the academy within “Winterveil,” a book that publisher HarperCollins has described as “The Secret History” meets “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.”

	“The thing about ‘Pokémon’ is that it works on so many different levels,” Reid says. “There’s a very low skill floor if you just want to engage in the main games and you beat the Elite Four and you catch all the Pokémon. It’s super fun. Pretty much anyone can do it. That’s the aspect of the game that’s marketed toward literal children, but then there’s also competitive Pokemon. It’s a turn-based strategy game, so like chess, but actually many orders of magnitude more complicated than chess. Wolfe Glick, who’s the most famous competitive ‘Pokémon’ player, he’s kind of like the [chess grandmaster] Magnus Carlsen of competitive ‘Pokémon,’ he said that competitive ‘Pokémon’ is like chess, but sometimes the pieces explode, which I think is a great way to explain it. It’s very chesslike. It’s strategic, it’s tactical, but it’s so much more complicated than that. There’s so many ways to customize your ‘Pokémon.’ There’s a lot of math and mathematical equations and probabilities and percentages. So that is the particular element that inspired aspects of ‘Winterveil,’ is competitive ‘Pokémon,’ specifically.”

	When she’s not playing competitive Pokemon, Reid has been hard at work on “Necromantica,” the sequel to her gothic fantasy epic “Innamorata.” After that massive cliffhanger in the first book, which released in March, there’s not much Reid can say yet about the sequel, which debuts next April, except that fan-favorite character Waltrude will certainly return.

	“Waltrude will be back,” Reid says. “She’s a POV character in the sequel, and Marozia is now a POV character in the sequel, which I think is obvious because she’s on the cover. But a large part of the story actually revolves around Gamelyn, who is the Master of Blood, who we’ve not seen very much in the first book. I don’t even think he’s had a line of dialogue, but he is a very, very significant character in the sequel and I’m very excited for that. I think his plot line and his chapters are some of the best things that I’ve ever written. Personally, I believe that, so I’m really excited.”
	

	Elsewhere, Reid is collaborating with “Room” writer Emma Donoghue on a film adaptation of Reid’s 2024 novel, “Lady Macbeth,” told from the point of view of the titular character herself.

	“We’re still pretty early. We’re still working on the script, but things are definitely moving along,” Reid says. “They’re moving along behind the scenes, as so many of these things do, which is kind of a hurry up and wait situation, similar to publishing.”

	Reid isn’t sure what the distribution plans for the film will be, but is not opposed to a streaming launch on the heels of the success of her filmmaker aunt Olivia Newman’s “Remarkably Bright Creatures” on Netflix. The TV movie was nominated for an Emmy at Monday’s awards show and star Sally Field took home the lead actress award in the category.

	“I don’t know if we’re even in the stage to be thinking about that,” Reid says. “I would prefer to have a theatrical release, I think, but my aunt’s movie just came out, ‘Remarkably Bright Creatures,’ and that was on Netflix and that has just done extraordinarily well in that format. So it’s definitely something I’m open to.”

schema.headline: How Competitive ‘Pokémon’ Inspired Author Ava Reid’s New Dystopian YA Series ‘Winterveil’

title: Viola Davis to Receive San Diego International Film Fest’s Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence – Film News in Brief
description: Viola Davis will be this year’s recipient of the Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence at the San Diego International Film Festival. Davis, an
body:
Viola Davis will be this year’s recipient of the Gregory Peck Award for Cinematic Excellence at the San Diego International Film Festival. Davis, an EGOT winner, is being honored for her work as an artist, activist, producer, philanthropist and New York Times bestselling author.

	“Viola Davis is one of the most extraordinary artists of our time,” Tonya Mantooth, CEO and artistic director of San Diego International Film Festival, said. “Her performances bring power, vulnerability and truth to every role, while her work beyond the screen has helped create opportunities for others. The Gregory Peck Award celebrates an enduring contribution to cinema, and Viola Davis embodies that legacy. We are honored to celebrate her remarkable artistry and impact.”
	

	The award, presented by Cecilia Peck, kicks off the 25th year of the festival and will be presented at the Night of the Stars Tribute on Oct. 13. The festival has also announced Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut” as the opening night film. The San Diego International Film Festival will take place from Oct. 13-18 in San Diego, California. Passes, tickets and additional festival information are available here.

	
		‘Princess Mononoke’ Returns to Theaters for Studio Ghibli Fest 2026	

	“Princess Mononoke,” from director Hayao Miyazaki, makes its return to theaters.

	The epic fantasy hits the big screen as part of GKIDS and Fathom Entertainment’s Studio Ghibli Fest 2026. A 4K restoration of the film will be in theaters from Sept. 26-30 in both the original Japanese and English-dubbed versions.
	

	The film follows young warrior Ashitaka who encounters a conflict between Lady Eboshi, the people of Iron Town and the mysterious Princess Mononoke. The English dub features the voices of Gillian Anderson, Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Minnie Driver, Jada Pinkett Smith and Billy Bob Thornton.

	The show dates are below.

	Saturday, Sept. 26 (English language dub)Sunday, Sept. 27 (English language dub)Monday, Sept. 28 (Japanese language with subtitles)Tuesday, Sept. 29 (Japanese language with subtitles)Wednesday, Sept. 30 (English language dub)

title: ‘Salvation’ Review: A Pin-Sharp Portrait of an Aspiring Life Coach in Personal Freefall
description: Our first impression of Danny Carlton, the callow protagonist of “Salvation,” is that he doesn’t look like a man you’d trust with your life. He’s yo
body:
Our first impression of Danny Carlton, the callow protagonist of “Salvation,” is that he doesn’t look like a man you’d trust with your life. He’s young, but that’s not the issue. It’s more the palpable air of uncertainty around him, evident in his shallow, darting gaze, his chummy but hesitant speech, his slightly gormless affect; he seems a nice enough lad, eager and solidly gym-built, but you wouldn’t readily hand him any greater responsibility than mowing your lawn. Appearances, of course, can be deceiving, but the great, growing sadness of Tom Nicoll‘s remarkable character study is that, in this case, they’re not. Danny is going nowhere, and just about everyone but him seems to know it, including his mentor and peers on the cockamamie life-coaching course that he thinks will finally make something of him.
	

	A quietly assured and impressive debut for Scottish writer-director Nicoll, “Salvation” is a timely work, in conversation with much recent discourse about the toxic pressures — social, physical and psychological — placed on GenZ men living heavily online. But the film doesn’t feel opportunistically ripped from the headlines. Danny, played with spiraling panic and desperately contrived machismo by a superb Liam Harkins, is a perceptively drawn, tragically human character rather than a representative construct of his time and age. And while his story says much about modern manosphere dynamics, it’s also heavily informed by more constant concerns of British class, gender and geographical difference. 


	There’s much thematic weight here, but balanced throughout with tension and humor — beginning with the all-too-real absurdism of the training retreat where we first meet Danny, and where self-styled life coach Marshall Allison (Kevin O’Loughlin) is fleecing young men for thousands of pounds with the promise that they’ll follow in his footsteps. There’s much jargon-y talk of unlocking freedom and earning potential, repeated with dead-eyed belief by Marshall’s protégés, some with more persuasive swagger than others. Danny is one of the unpersuasive ones, in part because he seems too honest for all this. “It’s not all about the money,” he argues, when Marshall critiques his salesmanship, only to be swiftly corrected by his teacher: “It kind of is.”
	

	Still, at the end of the weekend, Danny gets his certificate, because everyone does — and he returns home to Greenock, a post-industrial coastal town in the Scottish lowlands, an allegedly qualified life coach. Hey, it beats working in a pub, which is what he’s been doing up until now; all he needs is a bit of capital to set up his home office, build his website and secure some advertising, and once the clients come rolling in, he’ll pay back the loans in no time. 

	But apart from Scott (Stephen McMillan), an anxious, socially awkward 22-year-old with even less of a handle on the real world than Danny, no one’s really buying what he’s selling. A handful of other male applicants lose interest fast; he quickly drops his lone female client when she reveals more knowledge of e-commerce than he has. It turns out that even in this dubious professional field, some fakers are faker than others: Danny has mantras and breathing exercises, but no smell of success to him. And when the loan sharks come calling, his barely-a-business plan starts crumbling in wince-inducing fashion.

	In Harkins’ brilliantly twitchy, discomfiting performance, the terror of failure is written across Danny’s smooth, blokey face; so is the woebegone recognition of said failure in just about everything he does. We can hardly miss anything that Danny feels, fears or notices: Nicoll and DP Alex Grigoras shoot much of “Salvation” in tight, peering closeup, made all the more confrontational by the use of cramped Academy ratio throughout. It’s a formal choice that chimes with the character’s routine reliance on his phone’s front-facing camera to put his best face forward, whether in consultation with clients or attempting to hawk his skills on Instagram and TikTok. 

	Life offline could yet save Danny — Kathleen McDermott gives a wonderful, hard-bitten performance as his supportive but unsentimental mom Jackie, who wearily recognizes the limits of her influence — but there’s no promise in Nicoll’s relentlessly screw-tightening script that he’ll ever find his way there. There’s always another internet grift for someone looking to save himself fast, and without any gimmicky visual intrusions, the film feels authentically tuned into the aspirational mentality and oppressive reality of contemporary social media. There’s no need for of-the-moment hectoring or scare-mongering in “Salvation,” however; Danny’s arc on its own feels enough of a cautionary tale.

schema.headline: ‘Salvation’ Review: A Pin-Sharp Portrait of an Aspiring Life Coach in Personal Freefall

title: Cinelease Buys Up Grip and Lighting Gear From Quixote
description: Cinelease, the film equipment rental house, announced Tuesday that it is acquiring grip and lighting equipment from Quixote, which continues to shri
body:
Cinelease, the film equipment rental house, announced Tuesday that it is acquiring grip and lighting equipment from Quixote, which continues to shrink its footprint amid a production slump.

	Quixote announced in April that it was winding down its soundstage business, and is now getting out of the ancillary equipment business as well. The latest news means about 60 Quixote employees will be laid off, mostly in Los Angeles. 


	Cinelease, meanwhile, is looking to expand into sports and live events, as it grows beyond its base of servicing film and TV productions. The company is also buying up Quixote’s production supply assets, which will now go by the name Cinelease Pro Supplies, and has also purchased its portable restrooms and communications gear.
	

	“We see a significant opportunity to build Cinelease into a leading entertainment infrastructure platform,” said Louis Dargenzio, the company’s chairman, in a statement. “Our strategy is simple: invest in great people and complementary capabilities that make our customers’ jobs easier. Film and television will remain our foundation as we expand across live events, sports and large-scale projects. We will continue to invest in the capabilities that allow us to serve all of these markets at a greater scale.”

	Hudson Pacific Properties bought Quixote Studios for $360 million in 2022 — at the absolute peak of domestic film and TV production — and has since had to write off the entire investment. The company laid off 70 people earlier this year and got out of the soundstage business. It continues to operate one facility in Atwater Village, near Griffith Park, which remains under lease.
	

	Quixote also closed production services businesses in Atlanta, New Orleans, and Albuquerque, as it focused on its remaining services businesses in L.A. and New York. As the restructuring continues, Quixote is now focused on its transportation business, which includes Star Waggons trailers.

	Cinelease has also recently gotten into the rigging business with C&C Studio Services, now known as Cinelease Rigging; and has acquired barricades and fencing from West Coast Fencing.

	In the statement, Dargenzio said the firm will continue to partner with Quixote.

	“Quixote will continue to be a market leader in transportation, including its iconic Star Waggons brand,” he said. “We have tremendous respect for the people behind this business and what they’ve built.”

schema.headline: Cinelease Buys Up Grip and Lighting Gear From Quixote

title: Chuck Norris’ ‘Walker, Texas Ranger’ Co-Star Calls Emmys In Memoriam Snub a ‘Tragic’ and ‘Terrible Mistake’: ‘It Hurt My Feelings’
description: Chuck Norris‘ “Walker, Texas Ranger” co-star Judson Mills is speaking out about the Emmys decision to snub Norris from its In Memoriam tribute. Norr
body:
Chuck Norris‘ “Walker, Texas Ranger” co-star Judson Mills is speaking out about the Emmys decision to snub Norris from its In Memoriam tribute. Norris, who died in March at 86 years old, was a television icon in the 1990s as the star of the CBS procedural, which ran for nine seasons and 203 episodes between 1993 and 2001. The actor stayed with the show for its entire run and returned for the 2005 television movie “Walker, Texas Ranger: Trial by Fire.”
	

	In an interview with TMZ, Mills said the Emmys made a “terrible” and “tragic” mistake by leaving Norris out of the In Memoriam section. Mills played Francis Gage opposite Norris in the final two seasons of “Walker, Texas Ranger” and the “Trial by Fire” follow-up. 


	“Tragic mistake. And I have to assume it was just a terrible mistake. But my first thought was Gena and the family and his fans,” Mills said, referring to to Norris’ widow Gena O’Kelley.

	“I’m confident Chuck would encourage forgiveness. He was an ‘it’s not all about me’ kind of guy,” Mills continued. “But for an icon of his stature who impacted not only Hollywood, but the entire world, to see him not receive recognition at all and to see the family not receive that recognition was disappointing… It hurt my feelings for sure. He was a legend for God’s sake.”

	Norris was far from the only notable snub during the Emmys In Memoriam segment. “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” star Nicholas Brendon‘s name was not included on the screen during the tribute despite the ceremony including a “Buffy” reunion between Sarah Michelle Gellar and David Boreanaz earlier in the show. Also omitted were “Days of Our Lives” and “Starship Troopers” actor Patrick Muldoon, “The Gong Show” panelist Jaye P. Morgan, “The Ring” actress Daveigh Chase and “30 Rock” performer Grizz Chapman, among others.
	

	Norris’ death was announced by his family on March 20. The family wrote in a statement: “To the world, he was a martial artist, actor, and a symbol of strength. To us, he was a devoted husband, a loving father and grandfather, an incredible brother, and the heart of our family. He lived his life with faith, purpose, and an unwavering commitment to the people he loved. Through his work, discipline, and kindness, he inspired millions around the world and left a lasting impact on so many lives.”

schema.headline: Chuck Norris’ ‘Walker, Texas Ranger’ Co-Star Calls Emmys In Memoriam Snub a ‘Tragic’ and ‘Terrible Mistake’: ‘It Hurt My Feelings’

title: ‘Ace Combat 8’ Live-Action Prequel Star Josh Holloway on Revealing Four-Episode ‘Hour Zero’ Story Behind Bandai Namco Franchise’s New Game
description: Before “Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve” releases next month, fans of Bandai Namco Entertainment’s classic fighter-pilot video game franchise have a fe
body:
Before “Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve” releases next month, fans of Bandai Namco Entertainment’s classic fighter-pilot video game franchise have a few weeks of backstory to brush up on via live-action prequel project “Hour Zero.”

	Launching its first episode Tuesday, the four-installment short film is a first-of-its-kind project for the video game studio, which will reveal the plot going into the upcoming eighth “Ace Combat” game.
	

	Per Bandai Namco Entertainment America’s description for “Hour Zero”: “Three strangers survive the opening days of the Republic of Sotoa’s invasion of the Federation of Central Usea. Josh Holloway stars as a pilot with nowhere to land, Brandon Routh as a doctor who saved his enemy, and Tamlyn Tomita as a news anchor silenced for telling the truth. Told in reverse and grounded in the family lives of its three leads, their stories count down to the moment when their normal lives were shattered and war began. Their story sets the stage for the narrative players will experience in the deep, engaging Campaign Mode in ‘Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.’”


	The project was produced when “Ace Combat 8″ was already relatively far into the game development process, and Holloway had some questions before he agreed to join. Up to that point, his only experience working with a video game studio was voicing a character in 2007’s real-time strategy game “Command & Conquer 3: Tiberium Wars and that was cinematic footage for the game itself, not a live-action project.

	“At first I had a little reservation,” Holloway tells Variety. “I was like, a video game? I’m not sure. Because I’d done one a long time ago, but it was kind of on the cheesy side a little bit because it was just an internet game. It wasn’t a big thing. So I was a little nervous about it, but I loved this game as a teenager. I remember playing the first ‘Ace Combat’ games because they would be in the arcades with the big simulator, and I just loved it back then, and then I kind of went away from gaming for many, many years. So when they brought this up, I was like, I know this game, of all things, because I don’t know any games. And I’d seen ‘Maverick’ not long ago, so my interest was piqued again towards this type of genre, so I was really interested. I just had some immediate questions.”
	

	And once he saw the effort Bandai Namco planned to put into this, Holloway was sold.

	“I was like, ‘What’s the production value? I need to see a script. Do they have me sitting on an apple box with a toothpick in my hand, or is it an actual fuselage?’” Holloway says. “And when I got into it and found out how really well done and well prepared they were to do this, I was like, OK, this sounds like fun, and I can have my fighter pilot moment. Once I saw the production value and how he was going about it, I was like, oh yeah, I’m in. Let’s do this.”

	Set for release Oct. 2 across PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and PC, “Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve” takes place amid the lies, conspiracies and gossip that obscure the truth behind an ongoing war and the legendary ace fighting to reclaim the Federation of Central Usea from the Republic of Sotoa.

	“I wrapped around my character first, and the story and how he fit in that,” Holloway says. “So I was like, OK, I’m the OG pilot from way back. I’m a little older. I’m responsible for everybody. I’ve seen a lot of combat, a lot of death and I’m responsible for these kids. So that brings the stakes because I’m a father. I have children. I’m a leader. I’ve led for many years in my industry and stuff, so I understood all that. And also my father passed not long ago, so I really brought all the stakes. That’s what I had to do in my job as an actor. Now, what’s it going to look like?”

	Holloway and the Bandai Namco team worked with an actual fighter pilot to advise on the logistics of shooting.

	“Sometimes in a small frame, a lot of emotion and too much movement doesn’t translate,” Holloway says. “So how do I bring that intensity without going bananas and making it not work? Because this is a new thing for me, being inside a cockpit. How is he going to look when he’s making those turns. How much? How difficult is it? How many Gs are you pulling? What does it really feel like? It was amazing in our production that they had a real pilot there with me, and he’s telling me, ‘If you’re pulling that G, your body is actually gonna be grunting. You can’t even help it.’ I’m like, oh shit, really? So that was really amazing information to have on the layering of the look and the stakes that you’re bringing.”
	

	The “Hour Zero” story will continue to unfold across three more episodes (releasing Sept. 17, Sept. 23 and Sept. 29) before “Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve” is released.

schema.headline: ‘Ace Combat 8’ Live-Action Prequel Star Josh Holloway on Revealing Four-Episode ‘Hour Zero’ Story Behind Bandai Namco Franchise’s New Game

title: Danny Boyle Dodges AI Question About ‘Ink’ at TIFF: ‘I Don’t Think We’ll Need to Go Into That’
description: On Tuesday afternoon, Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” about the rise of U.K. tabloid The Sun under owner Rupert Murdoch (a cheeky Guy Pearce) and editor Larry
body:
On Tuesday afternoon, Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” about the rise of U.K. tabloid The Sun under owner Rupert Murdoch (a cheeky Guy Pearce) and editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell, swaggering), made its Canadian debut at the Toronto International Film Festival. As our critic wrote, it’s “a propulsive, can’t-look-away account” of the rise of the U.K.’s most popular tabloid and the smuttification of news, with the rag opting for outrageous headlines, giveaway contests and topless women over hard-hitting journalism. And yes, it’s indeed an electrifying film that should garner praise for not only Boyle but Pearce and Variety cover star O’Connell, who delivers his most magnetic performance since “Starred up.”
	

	During the film’s post-screening Q&A at the Princess of Wales Theatre, Boyle and the cast fielded questions from the audience about a few topics, including the movie’s use of AI. Boyle previously copped to using “about thirty seconds” of AI at the Telluride film Festival “where we animate a couple of old photographs.”


	“Oh, and there’s some mice,” he added. “It’s very good for animals and we had some mice that run around The Sun newsroom.”

	When an audience member in the balcony of the theater asked Boyle about his use of AI in the film and the threat AI poses more broadly to the film industry and the world, the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind TIFF-premiering “Slumdog Millionaire” said, “We used a tiny amount of it. It’s very much linked with VFX in our world; it’s one of the tools they use in the VFX. We try to be very responsible and make sure no actors were out of work because of it, so we would always employ actors if we were going to use a bit of it. There was about thirty seconds of it.”
	

	As for the broader implications of AI, he tabled that for another day.

	“The why of it… is a hugely complicated , which I don’t think we’ll need to go into here,” he offered. “But we will need to go into it, all of us.” With that, the moderator ended the Q&A.

	Boyle was joined onstage by O’Connell and Pearce who, earlier in the chat, dished on how they painted humanizing portraits of two larger-than-life figures who’ve wreaked quite a bit of chaos on the world. Boyle said he identified with the Yorkshire-raised Lamb because, as a native of Lancashire, he was also “an outsider coming to London.”

	Pearce, meanwhile, said that when he began researching Murdoch, he didn’t necessarily see the “monster” with the “mystique” that so many people paint him as, but someone timid and callow.

	“It started, really, with looking at some footage of Murdoch from the mid-‘60s onward,” Pearce explained of his fellow Aussie. “When I looked at footage of him and interviews of him where they would catch him at Sydney Airport or Melbourne Airport… he always looked awkward, he always looked shy, he always looked very humble… and not the image we all have of this person we think we now know given what we’ve seen in the last twenty, thirty or forty years.”

	He saw loads of “ambition” in Murdoch following his research, but mostly “a quiet, humble kind of chap.”

title: Why the Emmys Moving to Amazon Prime Video Won’t Fix What’s Broken With Award Shows
description:
Spoiler alert: Moving to streaming isn’t enough to fix award show problems.

	Mariska Hargitay closed the 78th Emmys on Monday night from the Peacoc
body:
Spoiler alert: Moving to streaming isn’t enough to fix award show problems.

	Mariska Hargitay closed the 78th Emmys on Monday night from the Peacock Theater, and the ceremony she sent off may be the last of its kind. Since 1949, the Emmys have belonged to broadcast television. Future editions may not.

	As Variety exclusively reported, the Television Academy is in advanced talks to move the show to Amazon Prime Video, taking the Emmys off broadcast television for the first time in history. TV Academy Chair Cris Abrego said only that “conversations are continuing.” This move would drop the Emmys into the same territory as the Oscars and SAG-AFTRA’s Actor Awards (the former heading to YouTube in 2029, the latter already on Netflix). Viewers will now require a subscription to tune in. Is that good or a bad thing?
	

	Under the most recent eight-year deal, struck in 2018, the networks paid just over $8 million a year for the rights to host the Emmys. Last year, that left CBS cutting an eight-figure check to stage a night that belonged to its streaming rivals. The 2025 telecast drew 7.59 million viewers, the best Emmy number since 2021. HBO Max, Apple TV and Netflix dominated the evening, while CBS took home a single one for the now-canceled “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert.” A tradition built on equity among the TV networks can turn into an expensive ritual that benefits platform competitors — and highlights how an individual distributor’s content failed to resonate.


	On paper, the Academy’s case for a single owner is a strong one. If you hand the Emmys to a platform that knows it will have them year after year, that platform has every reason to invest in the show, promote it and figure out what actually works. Under the “wheel” system, a network could pour money into a great telecast and then gift the audience it built to a rival the following fall. The Emmys never had the room to evolve in this way. One year is barely enough time to find the bathrooms at the Peacock Theater, let alone build an audience around a new idea.
	

	I wonder if the Academy remembers what happened the last time one company took control?

	An earlier wheel rotated the Emmys among ABC, CBS and NBC from 1966 to 1986. Then, in 1987, a hungry, low-rated Fox outbid the Big Three for exclusive rights. The ratings then cratered. One of those years didn’t have a host (1988), and went from nearly 36 million in 1986 to just over 12 million in 1990. The Emmys spent much of the next decade clawing back toward a shared model, in part because a television partner with a constant horse in the race had real value.

	An “agnostic” partner is hard to find, and that neutrality is difficult to defend when the networks themselves are no longer where a significant part of the audience lives. But dropping an awards show onto a streaming service does not necessarily make the audience grow.

	Look at the SAG Awards, now rebranded “The Actor Awards.” In 2024, the Screen Actors Guild moved its ceremony to Netflix, swapping TNT and TBS for the biggest streaming subscriber base on the planet. The result was 1.8 million views, roughly what the show pulled in its final year on cable. It missed Netflix’s weekly Top 10 in the U.S., but it did crack the Top 10 in Canada. In 2025, the ceremony was tighter, the reviews were better and the show brought Barbra Streisand to the podium for the Life Achievement Award. However, the audience still didn’t meaningfully spike, even with a global platform and hundreds of millions of subscribers. That doesn’t mean that it won’t grow over time. 

	I don’t think distribution was ever the dilemma awards shows were battling. The problem is that awards shows keep asking audiences to watch them the same way they always have, while audiences have moved on to evolving platforms. SAG drew 2.7 million viewers in 2019, then 2 million, then 1.8 million. The downslide was already underway before Netflix even entered the picture. But now, move a shrinking audience onto a bigger platform and it doesn’t suddenly grow without a reason for viewers to tune in (reminder: SAG, add supporting categories for TV and ensemble prizes for limited).



	

					Matthew Rhys at Sunday’s Emmy Awards.
									Getty Images
	



	The next year will be a make-or-break period that the TV Academy needs to take seriously if it wants to ensure its future for another 78 ceremonies. Last year, 7.59 million people watched the ceremony on CBS and the SAG Awards, on the world’s biggest streamer, drew roughly a quarter of that. It’s time to make some of the old guard uncomfortable with some meaningful changes.
	

	Amazon isn’t new to this — Prime Video has streamed the ACM Awards since 2022, making it the first major awards show to move to a streamer. But the Emmys are a different animal, and not only because they are bigger. Let’s remember also that Amazon has dogs in the TV awards fight.

	Prime Video landed 48 Emmy nominations this year and took home 10, including five for the now-canceled superhero series “Spider-Noir.” That hands the TV Academy a new wrinkle it cannot ignore: how do you guarantee the platform airing the Emmys doesn’t look like it’s playing with home-field advantage?

	During this year’s TV awards season, held on NBC, Variety heard frustration from various publicists and executives at rival studios over a decision to move five categories off the main telecast, which were dominated by streaming series, particularly HBO Max and Netflix. No one is suggesting those complaints point to impropriety, or that the Academy’s voting was somehow compromised. The TV Academy controls the ballot, through its third-party partner Ernst & Young, and its credibility rests on keeping that wall intact. But perception matters, especially when the company producing the telecast is also campaigning for the trophies being handed out.

	The Oscars’ deal with YouTube won’t carry quite that same baggage. Google doesn’t yet make prestige television. Prime Video does, campaigning for postapocalyptic drama “Fallout” and fantasy epic “Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” like every other studio. If Prime Video ever lands the next “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel,” the period comedy that once ran the table, rivals will scrutinize every decision around the telecast.

	And let’s also remember that streamers and broadcast networks don’t need nor want the same thing from the night.

	NBC wants an Emmy telecast that works as television, with a strong lead-in, a broad audience and plenty of advertising inventory. Amazon can think about the evening differently. Its ultimate goal is to serve Prime subscribers, keep viewers inside its ecosystem and stretch the ceremony into days of clips, interviews and social content.

	And that could be the real opportunity.

	The TV Academy is already trying to make the Emmys smaller and faster, shown by pushing five categories out of the main show. But once the ceremony lives on a platform where airtime isn’t dictated by a commercial break, why think smaller? Why not think bigger?
	

	The Creative Arts Emmys are split across two nights. So why not turn the whole celebration of television into an Emmys weekend, all 116 categories running Friday through Sunday? Give the Creative Arts ceremonies their own red carpets and live broadcasts (which they do not currently have). Make room for the meaningful speeches, and make room for all the creatives (aka artisans) whose work makes the shows being celebrated possible in the first place. Now it actually could make sense to include music performances from the nominated songs for music and lyrics. Now, you have the chance for viral moments.

	The artisans are not second-class citizens of this industry, though the telecast (and Hollywood in general) has relegated them away from the spotlight for decades. Amazon and the TV Academy can change that, because it doesn’t have to think like a network. They can firmly ask themselves what can make the viewers more invested and interested in these categories and crafts and then execute.

	But if the Academy is going to rethink where and how the Emmys are presented, it should take an equally hard look at how the awards themselves are structured. The problems are no longer confined to the telecast. They also live in the categories themselves, the ballots and, increasingly, the basic question of who even gets seen by the people voting. 



	

					John Mulaney during the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater.
									Trae Patton/NBC
	



	This calls for a real Emmys task force, one that pulls from across the industry sectors, rather than another small group charged with fixing one category at a time. Directors, writers, actors, editors, cinematographers, costume designers, sound professionals, craftspeople, reality performers and digital creators all deserve a seat at the table, alongside awards strategists and voters who understand how the rules actually play out once the ballots land. The mandate should be broad, with firm category definitions, nominee counts, peer-group voting, ballot presentation, eligibility and the widening gap between scripted, unscripted, limited, variety and digital programming. The point shouldn’t be to manufacture more trophies. It’s to make sure the work being judged is judged on a level playing field.

	Variety has floated plenty of ideas back in May 2025, from a reality performer category to a rethink of guest acting (again), standardized acting nominee counts, letting members opt into additional fields after certifying they’ve watched the work, a reconsidered limited series structure and pulling premium digital programming (i.e., creators and influencers) further into the Emmy fold. Some could work, and admittedly, others might not. But that’s exactly why the Academy needs to weigh them together, in an open forum and not one at a time. The Emmys need a full and comprehensive rules review that starts with a simple question: Does this system still make sense for the television industry we actually have?
	

	But of course, more time does not automatically equate to better time.

	As it stands, one-half of the EGOT foursome will have its own corner of the streaming universe. The Grammys are coming to ABC in 2027, while the Tonys appear to have a home on CBS, with a simulcast on Paramount+ to expand the audience. And if the Television Academy is going to bundle its show with a two-day shipping option, it could leave the Emmys right where they are now — only with fewer parachutes when things go wrong.

	Oh, and next year, get John Mulaney to host.

Raid on DTLA 'Stash House'
                          Feds Find Alligator, Pounds of Fentanyl
                          ... K-9 Collapses, Is Revived
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            1:18 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 15, 2026
                                2:11 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The feds raided a luxury apartment complex in downtown Los Angeles ... where a young couple ended up in custody after cops found pounds of fentanyl and cocaine -- and even a baby alligator, TMZ has confirmed.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Marvin Angelito and Susan Gonzalez were charged with possession with intent to distribute fentanyl. A search warrant was executed after a sting operation where the feds purchased drugs from an associate of Marvin and Susan.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Federal agents swarmed the DTLA apartment on September 10 ... and entered to find the two suspects sleeping. A K-9 was deployed to search the apartment but "became disoriented and began to collapse due to fentanyl exposure."
      
    
            The K-9 handler had to utilize Narcan to revive the police dog.
      
    
            The agents found 42,000 grams of fentanyl from the kitchen cupboard, 1,038 grams of heroin, three vials of bromobenzene, 7,000 grams of cocaine, and various tools to make drugs.
      
    
            The report said the agents also found an AR-15 rifle, a .50-caliber pistol, and a signal radio jammer device. A small alligator was also found and seized by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
      
    
            Homeland Security, the FBI, and the DEA were among the other agencies involved.

title: James Wehr Stopped By Cops Moments Before Fatal Crash, Was in Driver's Seat
description:
James Wehr
                          Pulled Over Before Deadly Crash ...
body:
James Wehr
                          Pulled Over Before Deadly Crash ...
                          Cops Confirm He Was Driving
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 15, 2026
                            2:47 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            James Wehr was behind the wheel of the McLaren that crashed and killed him Sunday ... and cops had actually stopped the vehicle earlier that night.
      
    
            A spokesperson for the Irvine Police Department tells TMZ ... Newport Beach Police Department stopped the McLaren before the fatal crash and gave the driver a warning.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            As we previously reported, Wehr was later driving the 2019 McLaren in Irvine when it crashed shortly after midnight. The impact split the McLaren apart and caused it to burst into flames, killing him and a 22-year-old woman.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            According to police, the vehicle was stopped at a red light near Culver Drive and Deerfield Avenue before accelerating northbound when the light turned green. The driver then lost control, veered off the road, hit a curb, and slammed into a tree.
      

        
                    
                  
      
    
            There has also been speculation online that a woman was behind the wheel of the McLaren, but an Irvine PD spokesperson tells TMZ ... "based on evidence, that just before the collision, a female was in the passenger seat and not the driver's seat." 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The second person in the McLaren has since been identified as 22-year-old Alexis "Lexi" Kramer. Her family confirmed her identity to us following the crash, explaining the two met via Instagram DM and Wehr flew Kramer out from Florida.
      
    
            Wehr was known in the Southern California car scene as the co-founder of South OC Cars and Coffee, a massive weekly gathering for automotive enthusiasts in San Clemente.
      
    
            The investigation remains ongoing, and police have not announced what specifically caused Wehr to lose control of the McLaren.
